reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard metabolic references
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive GM2 gangliosidosis caused by deficiency of the enzyme hexosaminidase A due to pathogenic variants in the HEXA gene
Carrier frequency is increased in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, making targeted carrier screening and prenatal diagnosis important
The classic infantile form presents around 3 to 6 months with loss of milestones, hypotonia progressing to spasticity, and an exaggerated startle response to sound
A cherry-red spot at the macula is a hallmark ophthalmological finding
Unlike many storage disorders, there is characteristically no hepatosplenomegaly, which helps distinguish it clinically
Progressive macrocephaly, seizures, blindness, and neurodegeneration follow, with death usually in early childhood
Juvenile and late-onset variants exist and can present with slower motor and psychiatric or cerebellar symptoms
No disease-modifying therapy is established, so management is supportive and genetic counselling is central
reference.pathophysiology: Tay-Sachs disease results from biallelic pathogenic variants in HEXA, which encodes the alpha subunit of the enzyme beta-hexosaminidase A. Deficient enzyme activity prevents degradation of GM2 ganglioside, which accumulates progressively within neuronal lysosomes of the central nervous system. Neuronal engorgement and dysfunction drive relentless neurodegeneration. Because storage is largely confined to neurons, visceral organomegaly is typically absent, distinguishing it from disorders such as Sandhoff disease, in which both hexosaminidase A and B are deficient.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of infantile neurodegeneration with cherry-red spot
additionalInvestigations: Assay of hexosaminidase A activity in serum or leukocytes
HEXA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and enable carrier detection
Ophthalmological examination for the macular cherry-red spot
Neuroimaging to characterise neurodegeneration and exclude alternatives
Carrier screening and prenatal or preimplantation testing for at-risk families
redFlags: Rapid developmental regression with exaggerated startle in an infant
Emerging seizures or loss of vision
Progressive swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
Family history in an at-risk population without prior carrier screening
reference.prognosis: The infantile form is progressive and fatal, typically within the first few years of life. Juvenile-onset disease progresses more slowly with death in later childhood or adolescence, while late-onset forms have a more variable and protracted course. Management remains supportive.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because hepatosplenomegaly is absent
Failing to distinguish it from Sandhoff disease, which additionally involves visceral storage
Not offering carrier screening to at-risk populations before conception
Attributing the exaggerated startle to a benign cause and delaying evaluation
management: Recognise there is no curative therapy, so care is supportive and palliative, centred on comfort and quality of life
Manage feeding difficulty and aspiration risk with feeding support and gastrostomy where needed
Treat spasticity and manage respiratory secretions and recurrent chest infections
Involve paediatric palliative care early for symptom control and family support
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across metabolic medicine, neurology and allied health
Offer genetic counselling with carrier screening, particularly in Ashkenazi Jewish families, and prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis for at-risk families
